2026 Proposed General Government Operating Budget

                 Appendix M
               Girdwood Valley Service Area
                             (Fund 106000)



The Municipality's Charter requires that our local government operate under a service area concept,
which means that residents of particular areas vote to levy taxes for service(s) from the Municipality.

Girdwood Valley Service Area was established for street construction and maintenance, solid waste
collection, fire protection, parks and recreation, the operation and maintenance of a municipal
cemetery, the provision of police protection services, and the provision of services in support of
policies that promote local housing and economic stability at the sole expense of the Girdwood
Valley Service Area. The maximum attainable mill rate for the service area shall not exceed 6.00
mills in any calendar year (AMC 27.30.020). The service area is included in Municipal Tax District 4.

The net cost total on the fund summary presented on the following page represents the tax cost for
the Girdwood Valley Service Area, based on the 2026 Proposed Budget.  It includes $79,201 of
revenues associated with the fund that are not considered program revenues, such as Penalties &
Interest (P&I) on Delinquent Taxes, Auto Tax, Electric Co-Op Allocation and Cash Pools Short-term
Interest.

The mill rate is calculated based on the taxes to be collected, divided by the assessed valuation of
the service area, then multiplied by 1,000.

              Taxes to be Collected in SA   x   1,000  =    Mill Rate
                Service Area Assessed Value

The preliminary 2026 mill rate, based on the 2026 Proposed Budget taxes to be collected and
preliminary service area assessed value at 08/27/2025, is calculated as follows:

                      $    5,465,561   x   1,000  =  5.55
                      $  984,704,946

The actual 2026 taxes to be collected and the actual 2026 mill rate will be based on the 2026
Revised budget that will include updated/revised IGCs and will be recalculated with updated
assessed values, all to be presented to the Assembly for approval in April 2026.

 1  AN ORDINANCE OF THE ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL ASSEMBLY UPDATING
 2  ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER  1.25, PUBLIC MEETINGS, AND
 3  AMENDING CHAPTER 4.05, AMC SECTIONS 2.30.030, 2.30.036, 2.40.035, 27.20.040
 4  AND 29.10.050, AND RELATED CODE CHANGES.
 5
 6  WHEREAS, the Anchorage Municipal Charter, Section 17.05(a), specifies that “…[a]ll
 7   meetings of the assembly, the school board and other boards and commissions shall be
 8   public” and that “[t]he assembly by ordinance shall adopt procedures for maximum
 9   reasonable public notice of all meetings.”; and
10
11  WHEREAS, the Municipality of Anchorage has enacted Chapter 1.25 of the Anchorage
12   Municipal Code, Public Meetings, to implement the Charter requirements and for a local
13   law corresponding to the State Open Meetings Act (AS 44.62.310-.319); and
14
15  WHEREAS, pursuant to, Alaska Statute 44.62.312, the policy of the State of Alaska
16   regarding meetings of governmental units such as the Municipality of Anchorage include
17   the following:
18        (a)(2): it is the intent of the law that actions of governmental units be taken openly and
19              that their deliberations be conducted openly;
20        (a)(3): the people of this state do not yield their sovereignty to the agencies that serve
21            them;
22        (a)(4): the people, in delegating authority, do not give their public servants the right to
23            decide what is good for the people to know and what is not good for them to
24           know;
25        (a)(5): the people's right to remain informed shall be protected so that they may retain
26              control over the government they have created…;
27
28  WHEREAS, pursuant to AS 44.62.310(a): “All meetings of a governmental body of a public
29    entity of the state are open to the public except as otherwise provided by this section or
30   another provision of law;” and
31
32  WHEREAS, pursuant to the Charter mandate and state law, over the past few decades the
33   Assembly has enacted minor changes to the Municipality’s Public Meetings code and
34   recognizes updates are needed to keep pace with changes in technology and increased
35   public interest and participation in Municipal meetings; and
36
37  WHEREAS, current AMC Chapter 1.25 and the Public Notice Manual published by the
38   Municipal Clerk contain provisions that need to be updated to reflect best practices and to
39  make  it easier for Municipal staff and the public to find public meeting information,
40    including:
41          the locations and procedures for physical public notice of meetings; and
42         updating the information to be included in minutes and recordings of public

                                      No. AM 620-2025

 1   From:     Assembly Chair Constant
 2
 3   Subject:   AN ORDINANCE OF THE ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL ASSEMBLY
 4           UPDATING ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER 1.25,
 5            PUBLIC MEETINGS, AND AMENDING CHAPTER  4.05, AMC
 6            SECTIONS 2.30.030, 2.30.036, 27.20.040 AND 29.10.050, AND
 7           RELATED CODE CHANGES.
 8
 9   This proposed ordinance is an omnibus update to the public meetings chapter of
10   the Anchorage Municipal Code, and other related code provisions. All municipalities
11   are required to comply with the state Open Meetings Act, AS 44.62.310 et seq., but
12  may have additional requirements or iterate provisions  for compliance.  This
13   ordinance seeks to:
14
15         update the language in the Code to be similar to the Open Meetings Act,
16          provide  consistency  between  assembly,  school  board,  boards  and
17         commissions, and LRSA Boards,
18           follow best practices with current technology, and
19          provide detailed information on how to follow the laws.
20
21   There are some updates specific to our local government structure and procedures.
22   Currently, the Anchorage Municipal Code speaks to public notice requirements in
23    relation to the different types of bodies and it is assumed that all bodies “advise the
24   public of  their meeting schedules, or publicly advertise  their meetings where
25   necessitated by statutory requirements.” Additionally, the Code doesn’t specify who
26    in relation to the board or commission is tasked with these responsibilities. The
27   sections of code relating to boards and commissions have not seen significant
28   updates since the mid-90’s; LRSA Boards, the code was brought forth from the
29   Greater Anchorage Area Borough Code.
30
31   While this looks like a big update, it’s more a big reorganization. Instead of speaking
32    to each type of body and the need to publicly notice the meeting, it spells out how
33    to notice meetings in AMC chapter 1.25 and provides that each type of body must
34   comply with that chapter. There are a few substantive changes to the duties of staff
35   and the requirement for an agenda and minutes. Changes are described fully in the
36   attached crosswalk.
37
38   There are some costs associated with the new requirement that all board and
39   commission meetings are to be recorded, for the purchase of additional audio
40   recording equipment that must be available to meet that requirement. However, the
41   Municipal Clerk estimates costs to the Municipality overall are less than $30,000,
42   therefor a summary of economic effects is not included.
